messages.subject: Re: about combined estimation
parts:
Hi All,

Gustavo's message started a series of emails between him, Steve Buckland, Jeff
Laake and I so I'll summarize the outcome in case anyone's interested.

In Gustavo's case, he has density estimates for two seasons and he wants to
calculate a mean density over both seasons. Note that the inference here will
be limited to the two seasons he sampled -- he's not going to make inferences
about the density in other seasons he didn't sample from. In stats language
this means treating season as a fixed effect.

An alternative would be if he had density estimates from a (large) number of
time periods, spread throughout the interval of interest. For example, if he
wanted to know average density over a whole year and he had sampled on 52 days
spaced at weekly intervals (i.e., a systematic random sample). In this case,
the 52 strata (time periods) could be regarded as a random sample of all the
time periods in the population (the 365 days in the year), and in calculating a
mean density for the year he'd be wanting to make inferences about the days he
didn't sample as well as the days he did. In stats language this means
treating time period as a random effect.

In both cases, calculation of mean density over strata is the same. But the
calculation of variance is quite different. (You can skip the next paragraph if
you don't want to know the details of this.)

Let stratum v have density estimate D_v, with estimated variance var(D)_v (by
variance I mean standard error of the estimate of D squared), and weight w_v
(for example if we weight by effort as Gustavo did). Let there be V strata in
total. For simplicity we'll assume the stratum estimates are independent (i.e.
no shared components such as estimate of f(0)) -- although the variance formulae
below easily generalize. Then the mean density over the strata is
D=sum(D_v*w_v)/sum(w_v)
For fixed effects the variance of mean density is a weighted average of the
stratum variances:
var(D)=sum(var(D)_v*w_v^2)/sum(w_v^2)
where w_v^2 means the weights squared. See Introduction to Distance Sampling
section 3.7.1 for examples of this when the strata are geographic areas.
Confidence intervals can be calculated using the log-normal method given in
equations 3.72-3.74, and the degrees of freedom for the t-statistic can be
calculated using the Satterthwaite approximation for a sum given on page 90
(which takes into account the degrees of freedom in each stratum).
For random effects the variance of mean density is calculated using the standard
formula for the variance of a weighted mean, assuming the strata are replicates:
var(D)=sum(w_v*[(D_v-D)^2])/(sum(w_v)*V-1)
For an example of this in a slighly different context, see Intro to Distance
Sampling, section 3.6.2 (formula 3.87). Confidence intervals are again
calculated using the log-normal method, but this time the degrees of freedom for
the t-statistic are simply V-1.

How does this relate to Distance? Well the Distance analysis engine has the
option to do either of these two analyses when you are calculating mean density
weighted by effort. But when I was constructing the graphical interface, I
didn't include the option to treat the strata as fixed. So when you choose to
weight by effort in the interface, Distance assumes you want to treat strata as
replicates (i.e., random effects).

So, that explains Gustavo's results: Distance was treating the two seasons he
surveyed as if they were a random sample from a large population of possible
seasons about which he wanted to calculate the mean density and confidence
intervals about the mean. The variance was calculated using the random effects
method I outlined above and the confidence intervals were calculated using a t-
statistic with 1 degree of freedom. Clearly a sample size of 2 strata is not
large for making inferences about the mean density, which is why the confidence
limits were wide. (Critical t-value for 1df and alpha=0.05 is 12.71 -- put that
into formula 3.73 (see text below the formula about using t rather than z
statistics) and you get wide intervals!) Gustavo kindly sent me his project
file, and since I have a slightly newer version of Distance than him I reran his
analysis and got similar results:

As you can see, the stratum estimates are unaffected, as are the pooled point
estimates. But now the degrees of freedom and confidence intervals are much
more reasonable.

I've changed the Distance interface to allow the option Gustavo wants to be
selected: there is now a "Strata are replicates" tick box on the Model
Definition | Estimate tab, which you tick for the first analysis and untick for
the second (it is ticked by default for backwards compatibility). I've also
updated the help file to make it clearer what Distance is doing when you choose
the various options on the Estimate tab. I hope to put out a new version of
Distance in the next few weeks and that will include this change.

So, thanks to Gustavo for helping improve the program through his question!

- Len

Postscript:
If you're desperate to do this analysis yourself, you'll have to run the
analysis engine as a stand-alone DOS program. Instructions for doing this are
in the program manual - look in the index under "Running analyses - running the
analysis engine as a stand-alone program". To get the input specifications you
want, I suggest the following procedure:
- get a stratified analysis set up in the Distance interface
- then from the main menu, choose Tools | Preferences | Analysis and tick the
box "Debug mode"
- run the stratified analysis. Distance will then produce an analysis engine
command and data file for you in your computer's temp directory (look in the log
tab of your analysis to see where Distance has put them).
- use some windows editor to edit the command file.
For the analysis where the strata are treated as replicates look for the line
Density=Stratum
and you want the options
Density=Stratum /Design=Replicate /Weight=Effort;
For the analysis where the strata are treated as fixed, you want
Density=Stratum /Design=Strata /Weight=Effort;
(Aside: one small difference you'll notice if you do this before I release the
next versin of Distance is that the N you get in the second case will be
different from the N I give above. That is because in the engine you have, when
/Design=strata, N is calculated as mean denstiy * sum(area of strata); I have
changed it to give mean denstiy * (area of stratum 1) which is more in keeping
with the other possible options here, and is also what's needed for analyses
like Gustavo's).
